body_html:
The clearest signs your insurance claim was underpaid are contractor bids well above the carrier's estimate, damaged areas missing from the scope, unexplained or heavy depreciation, pricing below local market rates, and missing items like overhead and profit, code upgrades or matching. If two or more apply, your settlement deserves a closer look.

What is an underpaid insurance claim?

An underpaid claim is one where the carrier accepted coverage and issued payment, but the amount does not reflect the real cost of repairing or replacing the covered damage. It is different from a denial. With a denial, the carrier says no. With an underpayment, the carrier says yes, just not enough.

Underpayment is often not obvious. The check arrives, the claim looks resolved, and the problem only surfaces when contractors start bidding or work begins. That is why it pays to review the estimate carefully before you sign anything or start repairs.

Underpayment does not always mean anyone acted in bad faith. Adjusters work under heavy caseloads after big storms, estimating software uses default pricing, and hidden damage is easy to miss on a single inspection. Whatever the cause, the result is the same: the payment falls short of what the policy promises.

10 signs your insurance claim was underpaid

1. Contractor bids are far higher than the insurance estimate

If multiple reputable contractors come in well above the carrier's number, that is the strongest early warning sign. One high bid may be an outlier. Three consistent bids that all exceed the estimate usually point to a real scope or pricing gap.

2. Damaged areas are missing from the scope

Compare the estimate to what you actually see. Are all roof slopes included? Every damaged elevation of siding? Interior ceilings with water stains? Fences, gutters, screens and outbuildings? Missing rooms or components are among the most common causes of underpayment.

3. The estimate calls for repair when replacement is needed

Spot repairs on a roof with widespread hail damage, or patching a section of flooring that runs continuously through several rooms, may not produce a proper repair. See why insurance estimates are often lower for the reasons this happens.

4. Depreciation looks excessive or unexplained

Depreciation reduces your actual cash value payment based on age and condition. If a well-maintained roof is depreciated as if it were near the end of its life, or depreciation is applied to labor where the policy and state practice do not support it, your first payment may be too low. Learn more about recoverable depreciation.

5. Unit prices are below local market rates

Estimating software prices vary by region and update over time, but they do not always reflect post-storm demand. If labor and material prices in the estimate are below what contractors in your area actually charge, the total will be short.

6. Overhead and profit were left out

When a repair reasonably requires a general contractor to coordinate multiple trades, overhead and profit (often 10 percent each in industry practice) may belong in the estimate. Leaving it out can reduce the claim significantly on multi-trade jobs.

7. Necessary line items are missing

Roof claims often miss items such as drip edge, starter strips, ridge cap, flashing, vent boots, permits, steep and high charges, and debris removal. We list the usual suspects in common Xactimate line items missing from roof claims.

8. Code upgrades were ignored

If your city requires upgrades to complete the repair and your policy includes ordinance or law coverage, those costs may be payable. An estimate that prices the repair as if current code did not exist may be incomplete.

9. Matching was not addressed

Replacing a few shingles or siding panels that no longer match the rest of the house can leave an obvious patchwork. Depending on policy wording and the circumstances, matching may justify a broader repair.

10. The adjuster spent very little time on site

A quick inspection, especially one that skipped the attic, interior or certain roof slopes, increases the chance that damage was missed. If you were not present, ask for the inspection photos and notes.

Understanding the causes helps you target your response. The most common reasons include:

An example of an underpaid roof claim

Here is an illustrative example of how the signs above add up. The figures are hypothetical, but the pattern is one we see often.

A homeowner's roof is hit by hail. The carrier's estimate replaces two slopes and pays $9,500 after a $2,500 deductible and depreciation. Three local roofers each bid a full replacement between $17,000 and $19,000. When the homeowner compares the documents, several gaps appear:

  • The estimate measured the roof at 24 squares, while the contractor measured 28 squares plus waste.
  • Two damaged slopes facing the storm's direction were not included.
  • Drip edge, starter, ridge vents and flashing were missing.
  • No overhead and profit was included even though gutters, screens and a fence also needed work.
  • Depreciation treated a 9-year-old roof as if it were near the end of its life.

None of these items is unusual on its own. Together, they explain most of the gap between the carrier's number and the contractor bids. Measurement differences alone can matter a lot, which is why we built a free roof square calculator so homeowners can sanity-check the numbers.

In a case like this, the homeowner would typically start by sending the bids, photos and a list of missing items to the adjuster. If the carrier will not revise the estimate, appraisal becomes a practical next step because the dispute is about measurements, scope and price rather than coverage.

How to review your insurance estimate

You do not need to be an estimator to spot problems. Work through the estimate with these steps:

  1. Get the full line-item estimate. A summary page or payment letter is not enough. Ask for the complete estimate with quantities and unit prices.
  2. Walk the property with the estimate in hand. Check each room, elevation and roof slope against what is listed.
  3. Check measurements. Roof squares, wall areas and flooring square footage should match reality. Our roof tools can help.
  4. Compare against contractor bids. Look line by line for items your contractor included and the carrier did not.
  5. Review depreciation. Note how much was withheld and whether it is recoverable after repairs.
  6. Read the policy. Check for replacement cost terms, ordinance or law coverage, matching language and the appraisal clause.
Tip: Keep all communication with your carrier in writing, or follow phone calls with a short email summarizing what was said. A clear written record helps in negotiation, supplements and appraisal.

What to do if your insurance claim was underpaid

Once you have identified the gap, you have several options. They are not mutually exclusive, and many homeowners use more than one.

Request a re-inspection and submit documentation

Send the carrier your photos, contractor estimates and a written list of missing or underpriced items. Ask them to reinspect and revise the estimate. Many underpayments are corrected at this stage.

File a supplemental claim

If additional damage is discovered during repairs, a supplement asks the carrier to add it to the claim. See supplemental insurance claims explained for how this works.

Invoke appraisal

If the carrier accepts coverage but will not move on the amount, most Texas property policies let either side demand appraisal. Each side names an appraiser, an umpire decides disagreements, and the award sets the amount of loss. Our guide on how to fight a low insurance settlement walks through each option in more depth.

File a complaint or seek legal advice

Texas policyholders can file a complaint with the Texas Department of Insurance. If you believe the carrier violated Texas Insurance Code chapters 541 or 542, speak with a Texas attorney. This is general information, not legal advice.

Underpaid insurance claims in Texas

Texas homeowners face frequent hail and wind events, and storm seasons bring a surge of claims that can stretch adjusters thin. In Austin, Dallas, San Antonio and across Central and North Texas, it is common for roof claims to come in low on the first pass because of missed slopes, missing accessories or pricing that does not reflect post-storm demand.

Texas law gives policyholders useful protections. Chapter 542 sets deadlines for carriers to acknowledge, decide and pay claims. Chapter 542A generally requires 61 days' written notice before filing suit on a weather-related claim. And the appraisal clause gives you a way to resolve amount-of-loss disputes without going to court. Homeowners in Central Texas can learn more on our Austin insurance appraiser page.

Next steps if you think you were underpaid

Do not assume the first payment is final. Gather your estimate, policy, photos and contractor bids, then compare them carefully using the signs above. If the gap is meaningful and the carrier will not adjust, appraisal is often the most efficient path to a fair amount.

faqs.q: How do I know if my insurance settlement is too low?
faqs.a: Compare the carrier estimate line by line with at least two or three contractor bids and with the damage you can see. Large, consistent gaps, missing rooms or roof slopes, low unit prices and heavy depreciation all suggest the settlement may be too low. A professional estimate review can confirm it.

faqs.q: Can I reopen an insurance claim if I was underpaid?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Many carriers will reconsider a claim when you submit new evidence, such as photos, contractor bids or hidden damage found during repairs. Policy deadlines and Texas law still apply, so act promptly. In some cases appraisal can also be invoked after payment if the amount of loss remains disputed.

faqs.q: Should I cash the check if I think my claim was underpaid?
faqs.a: In many cases, cashing an undisputed payment does not by itself end your right to seek more, but wording on checks and release forms matters. Read any document before signing. If a check or letter says it is a full and final settlement, consider getting advice before depositing it.

faqs.q: How long do I have to dispute an underpaid claim in Texas?
faqs.a: It depends on your policy and the law. Many Texas policies set a deadline to sue, often two years and one day from when the claim accrued, and chapter 542A generally requires 61 days of pre-suit notice for weather claims. Check your policy and talk with an attorney about specific deadlines.

faqs.q: Is appraisal a good option for an underpaid claim?
faqs.a: Appraisal works well when the carrier agrees the damage is covered but disputes how much it costs to fix. It is usually faster and less expensive than litigation. It is less useful when the dispute is purely about coverage, since Texas appraisers decide the amount of loss rather than coverage questions.
